chunks.title: About Muhammad Ibrahim Khan
chunks.text: Muhammad Ibrahim Khan publishes as Ibrahim Khan. Public names: Muhammad Ibrahim Khan, Ibrahim Khan. Reinforcement Learning, Planning and Research Software. PhD researcher at Coventry University and Research Software Developer at UCL, working on reinforcement learning, planning, reliable control and reproducible AI research software. I develop learning and planning methods for energy-efficient building control, with a particular focus on Monte Carlo Tree Search, PPO and SAC. My research also studies interpretable policies and the numerical behaviour that can make reinforcement learning unreliable. At UCL, I build reproducible experimental software for multi-agent LLM research.

chunks.title: Current research and software work
chunks.text: I am currently working across three connected areas: planning and reinforcement learning for energy control, reliable reinforcement-learning experiments, and reproducible software for multi-agent LLM research. The common thread is making sequential AI systems easier to evaluate, audit and explain.

chunks.title: Planning for energy-aware control
chunks.text: Status: Active research. Research question: How can a controller look ahead, meet time and comfort constraints, and avoid unnecessary energy use when future conditions are uncertain? Current focus: Comparing planning and reinforcement-learning approaches for building heating and domestic hot-water control, using MCTS, PPO, SAC and BOPTEST. Why it matters: A useful controller must balance efficiency with operational reliability; average reward alone does not show whether deadlines or constraints were actually met.

chunks.title: Reliable reinforcement learning
chunks.text: Status: Active research. Research question: Which numerical and experimental details can change policy optimisation, and how can those effects be isolated without overstating the evidence? Current focus: Running controlled comparisons, checking policy and task behaviour separately, and keeping a traceable route from each conclusion to its supporting run. Why it matters: Small implementation details can undermine a comparison if they are not measured and reported explicitly. Public scope: Only the broad public research direction is described here. Details tied to anonymous review or unpublished results are withheld until public.

chunks.title: From deadlines to decisions: a planning view of hot-water control
chunks.text: Why domestic hot-water control becomes a useful planning problem once deadlines, uncertainty and energy use are considered together. A domestic hot-water heater looks simple: switch it on, wait, and switch it off. The control problem becomes more interesting when the water must be ready by a deadline, electricity conditions change, and unnecessary heating carries a cost. This is one of the problems I use to study planning and reinforcement learning. It is small enough to explain clearly, but still contains the parts that make real control decisions difficult: delayed effects, uncertain demand, constraints and competing objectives. Why the deadline matters A controller that only reacts to the current temperature can miss the reason for heating. The useful question is not simply “is the water cold?” It is: > Which action now gives a good chance of meeting the required temperature at > the required time without using more energy than necessary? That phrasing changes the task from a thermostat rule into a planning problem. The controller needs a model of how temperature evolves, a description of the deadline and an objective that makes the trade-off explicit. What a planning controller considers In a tree-search formulation, each branch represents a possible sequence of future actions. Simulated trajectories estimate what could happen after those actions, and the search allocates more attention to promising branches while continuing to explore alternatives. For this kind of study, the important pieces are: the state available to the controller; the actions it is allowed to take; the thermal model and uncertainty assumptions; the deadline and comfort requirement; the energy objective; and the baseline controllers used for comparison. The algorithm name is only one part of the experiment. Without the rest of that specification, it is difficult to tell what a result means or whether it would reproduce. Comparing methods fairly My public work examines planning and reinforcement-learning approaches, including Monte Carlo Tree Search, PPO and SAC. A useful comparison keeps the task, observations, action limits and evaluation conditions aligned. It also reports failures and constraint violations rather than reducing everything to one reward number. This matters because different controllers can succeed in different ways. A method may meet the deadline reliably but consume more energy; another may be efficient on average but fail in difficult conditions. Those outcomes should remain visible in the evaluation. Making the experiment auditable I treat reproducibility as part of the research method rather than a final cleanup step. In practice, that means recording configuration, seeds, environment conditions and output summaries; checking that comparisons differ only where intended; and keeping a clear route from a claim back to the run that supports it. The broader lesson is useful beyond hot water. When an AI controller acts over time, the quality of the conclusion depends as much on the experimental design as on the learning or planning algorithm. You can read the public paper, “Deadline-Aware, Energy-Efficient Control of Domestic Immersion Hot Water Heaters”, explore the hot-water control repository, or try the smaller planning examples on the interactive demos page.

chunks.title: Some projects I have made public
chunks.text: A quick look at a few of my public GitHub projects. I spend a lot of time working on research, but I also like making smaller projects around the same ideas. They help me test things properly and, most of the time, they make a difficult idea much easier to understand. Here are a few projects that I have made public on GitHub. Some are closely related to my research and some are just useful things I wanted to build. RL for HVAC Teaching a controller to keep a home comfortable while responding to changing energy prices. View on GitHub → Hot water control Comparing planning and reinforcement learning for heating water on time while using less energy. View on GitHub → Meeting transcriber A small tool that turns meeting audio into transcripts, notes and action points. View on GitHub → MCTS Tic-Tac-Toe A simple game where you can play against an AI that plans its moves using tree search. View on GitHub → What connects them? The energy projects are about making better choices when we do not know exactly what will happen next. The Tic-Tac-Toe project shows the same planning idea in a much smaller and more visual problem. The meeting transcriber is a bit different. I made it because long supervision meetings can contain a lot of useful details, and it is easy to forget a small action point afterwards. The tool keeps the audio private during transcription, then turns it into notes which are easier to use. I will keep adding to these repos when I have something useful to share. You can also see the rest of them on my GitHub.

chunks.text: Reinforcement learning trains an agent to choose actions by learning from the consequences of earlier decisions. Why it is relevant here: Ibrahim uses it for sequential control problems where heating decisions affect later comfort, deadlines and energy use.

chunks.title: Monte Carlo Tree Search
chunks.text: Monte Carlo Tree Search, or MCTS, looks ahead by simulating possible action sequences and spending more search effort on promising choices while still exploring alternatives. Why it is relevant here: It is a central planning method in Ibrahim's PhD and appears in his hot-water, heat-pump and Tic-Tac-Toe work.

chunks.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
chunks.text: Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, is a policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm that limits how far a policy changes during each update. Why it is relevant here: Ibrahim uses PPO in building-control research and studies how numerical details can make policy optimisation unreliable.

chunks.title: Soft Actor-Critic
chunks.text: Soft Actor-Critic, or SAC, is an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm for continuous actions. It reuses past experience and balances reward with continued exploration. Why it is relevant here: Ibrahim uses SAC for continuous heating-control experiments, including the public HVAC project.

chunks.title: BOPTEST
chunks.text: BOPTEST is a building-control benchmark that exposes realistic simulated buildings through a common test interface. Why it is relevant here: It lets Ibrahim compare learned and conventional heating controllers under aligned weather, comfort and energy conditions.

chunks.title: Reproducible and auditable research
chunks.text: Reproducible research records enough configuration, data conditions and outputs for another person to repeat the procedure. Auditable research also keeps a traceable route from a claim back to its evidence. Why it is relevant here: Ibrahim treats this as part of experiment design, not as a final cleanup step.

chunks.title: Planning versus learned control
chunks.text: A planning controller searches possible futures when it acts, while a learned controller trains a policy in advance and then applies it quickly. Neither is automatically better in every setting. Why it is relevant here: Ibrahim compares the two under the same task and reports deadline, comfort and energy outcomes separately.
